questions.scenario: A 68-year-old woman has had an itchy, red and white plaque on the vulva for years that was treated as eczema. A biopsy shows large pale cells with abundant cytoplasm scattered among the keratinocytes of the epidermis, with no invasion into the dermis.
questions.lead_in: Why does the surgeon plan a wide local excision, and what is the risk if margins are narrow?
questions.stem: Why does the surgeon plan a wide local excision, and what is the risk if margins are narrow?
options: The plaque is a benign sweat gland tumor, so a wide margin prevents regrowth of a dermal nodule
The lesion is HPV related and multifocal, so wide excision removes all infected skin
The malignant cells spread laterally within the epidermis, so excision can be incomplete and the disease may recur
The cells have invaded deep stroma, so a wide margin is needed to reach nodal disease
The lesion is a thin sclerotic patch, so wide excision prevents loss of the labia
choice_rationales: A benign dermal sweat gland tumor is papillary hidradenoma and would not be managed this way.
Paget disease is not an HPV driven multifocal lesion, which describes classic VIN.
Lateral intraepidermal spread is the reason for wide margins and for recurrence.
The disease is typically confined to the epidermis, so deep stromal and nodal spread is not the usual picture.
Sclerosis and loss of labia describe lichen sclerosus, not this plaque.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Large pale cells within the epidermis in an itchy red and white plaque is vulvar (extramammary) Paget disease, an intraepithelial neoplasm. Step 2. The lecture states that Paget cells spread laterally, so excision may be incomplete and the disease may recur, which is why wide local excision is the treatment. Invasion is rare, and poor prognosis follows when it does occur.
visual_clues: The epidermis is the darker band along the top.
Several pale cells are larger than the adjacent keratinocytes.
questions.visual_target: Pale atypical cells in the epidermis

questions.condition_overview: Extramammary Paget disease is an uncommon intraepidermal adenocarcinoma, most often on the vulva of older women, that presents as a red, scaly or eczematous, itchy plaque. Microscopically large pale cells with abundant cytoplasm and atypical nuclei are scattered singly and in nests among the keratinocytes of the epidermis, sometimes extending into skin appendages. The cells contain intracytoplasmic mucin (mucicarmine and PAS positive) and are CK7 positive, unlike squamous cells. It is usually confined to the epidermis, but some cases are associated with an underlying adnexal or visceral carcinoma, and the invasive form carries a worse prognosis. Treatment is wide excision.

questions.scenario: A 70-year-old woman has a pruritic, painful, erythematous vulvar plaque. A biopsy shows an intraepithelial proliferation of malignant cells larger than the surrounding keratinocytes with pale cytoplasm. A medical student recalls that Paget disease of the nipple is often linked to an underlying cancer.
questions.lead_in: How does this vulvar disease usually differ from Paget disease of the nipple?
questions.stem: How does this vulvar disease usually differ from Paget disease of the nipple?
options: It arises from a preexisting HPV related condyloma
It is typically an in situ intraepithelial neoplasm not associated with an underlying cancer
It is a benign glandular tumor with myoepithelium
It is always associated with an underlying invasive adenocarcinoma of the rectum
It is a premalignant lesion that always progresses to squamous carcinoma
choice_rationales: Condyloma is a separate HPV related exophytic lesion, not the origin of Paget cells.
The lecture states it is typically in situ and not associated with underlying cancer.
A benign glandular tumor with myoepithelium describes papillary hidradenoma.
The lecture does not describe an obligate underlying rectal carcinoma.
Paget cells are malignant and the process is not described as a squamous precursor.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Large pale malignant cells confined to the epidermis identify vulvar Paget disease. Step 2. The lecture contrasts it with Paget disease of the nipple by noting that the vulvar form is typically in situ and not associated with underlying cancer. Cells are thought to arise from multipotent cells in the mammary-like gland ducts of vulvar skin, and invasion or metastasis is rare but carries a poor prognosis.
visual_clues: Use the level of the atypical cells and their pale cytoplasm together.

questions.scenario: A pathologist examines a vulvar plaque biopsy containing scattered large pale cells in the epidermis. A histochemical stain shows bright cytoplasmic positivity in these cells but not in the neighboring keratinocytes.
questions.lead_in: What does this result indicate about the cells, and how does it affect the diagnosis?
questions.stem: What does this result indicate about the cells, and how does it affect the diagnosis?
options: Fungal hyphae in the keratin layer, which indicates candidiasis
Myoepithelial cytoplasm, which indicates papillary hidradenoma
Intracytoplasmic mucin in malignant cells, which confirms Paget disease
Glycogen in normal clear keratinocytes, which excludes neoplasia
Keratin pearls from invasive squamous carcinoma
choice_rationales: Candida is shown on PAS in the thickened keratin layer, not in epidermal cells.
Hidradenoma shows myoepithelium, which is shown with calponin, SMA, and EMA, not mucin.
Mucin positive pale cells confirm Paget disease according to the lecture.
The cells that stain are malignant and are not described as normal keratinocytes.
Keratin pearls are not the finding with intracellular mucin.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Positive cytoplasmic staining of the large pale cells with mucin stains (mucicarmine or diastase PAS) shows that the cells contain mucopolysaccharide. Step 2. The lecture states this staining confirms the diagnosis of Paget disease. The stain is positive in the atypical cells and not in the surrounding keratinocytes, which is why it helps classify the conspicuous cells.
visual_clues: Locate the pink material within individual cells rather than along the surface or in the dermis.

questions.tested_concept: Which precursor lesion and molecular change most likely preceded this carcinoma?
questions.visual_target: Vulvar plaque and the evidence for stromal invasion
questions.scenario: A 74-year-old woman with long-standing lichen sclerosus has a firm, ulcerated vulvar lesion. A biopsy shows irregular nests of keratinizing squamous cells in the stroma beneath the surface. The tumor is HPV negative.
questions.lead_in: Which precursor lesion and molecular change most likely preceded this carcinoma?
questions.stem: Which precursor lesion and molecular change most likely preceded this carcinoma?
options: Extramammary Paget disease with mucin positive cells
Differentiated vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia with p53 mutation
Classic VIN with high risk HPV type 16
Condyloma acuminatum with koilocytes
Papillary hidradenoma with myoepithelium
choice_rationales: Paget disease is an intraepithelial glandular process, not a squamous precursor.
HPV negative carcinoma in an older patient with lichen sclerosus fits differentiated VIN and p53 mutation.
Classic VIN is HPV 16 related and tends to occur in younger women, which does not fit.
Condyloma is a benign exophytic HPV lesion and is not the described precursor.
Hidradenoma is a benign sweat gland tumor and is not a carcinoma precursor.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Nests of squamous cells invading the stroma are invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Step 2. The lecture states about 70 percent of vulvar carcinomas are unrelated to HPV and arise from differentiated VIN in older women, linked to lichen sclerosus or squamous hyperplasia and p53 mutation, giving keratinized squamous carcinomas. The 30 percent related to HPV arise from classic VIN and form basaloid and warty carcinomas.
visual_clues: Irregular epithelial nests lie in the underlying stroma.
questions.ground_truth_basis: Visible findings in the cited learner image interpreted with the cited teaching pages.
questions.condition_overview: Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma has two main pathways. HPV-related tumors arise from usual-type VIN in younger women and are basaloid or warty. HPV-independent tumors arise from dVIN or lichen sclerosus in older women and are keratinizing. Keratinizing tumors show irregular nests of atypical squamous cells with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges invading dermis. Depth of invasion, tumor size, and groin node status determine stage and prognosis. Treatment is wide excision, and groin node assessment is needed when invasion exceeds 1 mm.

questions.tested_concept: Which pairing correctly separates the older patient's lesion from the younger patient's?
questions.visual_target: Vulvar plaque differential at the epithelial base
questions.scenario: A 66-year-old woman has a single white vulvar plaque next to an area of lichen sclerosus. Biopsy shows atypical cells concentrated at the base of the epithelium, while the upper layers mature normally. A resident compares her to a 30-year-old smoker with multifocal lesions and prior CIN.
questions.lead_in: Which pairing correctly separates the older patient's lesion from the younger patient's?
questions.stem: Which pairing correctly separates the older patient's lesion from the younger patient's?
options: Older patient has extramammary Paget disease, younger patient has squamous hyperplasia
Older patient has condyloma, younger patient has lichen sclerosus
Older patient has HPV 16 related classic VIN, younger patient has differentiated VIN
Both have classic VIN because basal atypia is always HPV related
Older patient has HPV negative differentiated VIN with p53 mutation, younger patient has HPV related classic VIN
choice_rationales: Paget disease and squamous hyperplasia do not match basal atypia with maturation.
Condyloma and lichen sclerosus are benign and do not match the biopsy descriptions.
The age and unifocal pattern are reversed in this option.
Basal atypia with preserved maturation is differentiated VIN, which is not HPV related.
The lecture ties older, unifocal, lichen sclerosus related disease to differentiated VIN with p53 mutation.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Basal atypia with maturation above, unifocal, in an older woman with lichen sclerosus is differentiated VIN (VIN simplex). Step 2. The lecture lists differentiated VIN as HPV negative, older age, unifocal, associated with inflammation, lichen sclerosus or squamous hyperplasia, and p53 mutation. Classic VIN is HPV 16 related, younger, multifocal, associated with CIN and VAIN, with lack of maturation and basaloid cells.
visual_clues: The deepest epithelial cells are conspicuously atypical while the superficial layers still mature.
questions.ground_truth_basis: Visible findings in the cited learner image interpreted with the cited teaching pages.
questions.condition_overview: Differentiated VIN is an HPV-independent precancer of the vulva that occurs in older women and is typically associated with lichen sclerosus or lichen planus. The atypia is confined to the basal and parabasal layers, with premature keratinization and maturing, eosinophilic superficial cells that make it easy to overlook. Mutated p53 is often present. dVIN is the usual precursor of HPV-independent keratinizing vulvar squamous cell carcinoma and progresses rapidly, so it is excised.

options: A stain for dermal collagen sclerosis
PAS for fungal hyphae in keratin
Calponin for myoepithelium
Mucicarmine or diastase PAS for intracellular mucin
p53 immunostain for mutation
choice_rationales: Collagen sclerosis is the lichen sclerosus pattern.
PAS for hyphae is a different use for candidiasis.
Calponin shows myoepithelium in hidradenoma.
Mucin stains demonstrate the cytoplasmic mucopolysaccharide of Paget cells.
p53 mutation is associated with differentiated VIN.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Large pale cells in the epidermis of an eczema like plaque are Paget cells. Step 2. The lecture states that positive cytoplasmic staining with mucicarmine or diastase PAS confirms the diagnosis because the cells contain mucopolysaccharide. Calponin is for hidradenoma and p53 relates to differentiated VIN.
visual_clues: Choose mucicarmine to demonstrate cytoplasmic mucin in the large pale intraepidermal cells.

questions.scenario: A 48-year-old woman has weight loss, tremor, and heat intolerance. Her TSH is suppressed, but a thyroid scan shows no thyroid nodule. Pelvic imaging shows a unilateral ovarian mass. The ovarian section shows round follicles filled with dense eosinophilic colloid.
questions.lead_in: Which explanation accounts for her hyperthyroid symptoms?
questions.stem: Which explanation accounts for her hyperthyroid symptoms?
options: A Krukenberg tumor is releasing mucin that mimics TSH
Functioning thyroid tissue within the ovarian tumor, a monodermal teratoma, is producing thyroid hormone
A granulosa cell tumor is secreting inhibin that stimulates the thyroid
A yolk sac tumor is secreting alpha fetoprotein with thyroid stimulating activity
A dysgerminoma is producing thyroid hormone from fibrous septa
choice_rationales: Krukenberg tumors are metastatic signet ring tumors and do not make thyroid hormone.
Struma ovarii is a monodermal teratoma with thyroid elements that can cause hyperthyroidism.
Inhibin is a marker of granulosa cell tumor and does not stimulate the thyroid.
Alpha fetoprotein is a yolk sac marker and has no thyroid stimulating role in the lecture.
Dysgerminoma is a germ cell tumor of large primitive cells and is not thyroid tissue.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Follicles filled with colloid in an ovarian tumor are thyroid tissue, so this is struma ovarii. Step 2. The lecture lists struma ovarii among specialized monodermal teratomas, which contain only thyroid elements (follicles and colloid), and notes that they may cause hyperthyroidism. A suppressed TSH with a normal thyroid gland fits an ectopic source.
visual_clues: Look for the thin cellular rims around the dense pink centers.
questions.visual_target: Rounded follicles containing dense colloid
questions.tested_concept: Which explanation accounts for her hyperthyroid symptoms?

questions.condition_overview: Struma ovarii is a monodermal form of ovarian teratoma composed predominantly (more than half) of mature thyroid tissue. It forms thyroid follicles filled with eosinophilic colloid, and it can rarely cause hyperthyroidism or undergo malignant change. Most cases are benign and are treated by surgical resection.

questions.scenario: A 40-year-old woman has a unilateral ovarian mass removed. The pathologist reports that most of the tumor is mature thyroid follicles with colloid and cannot find skin, cartilage, or neural tissue after thorough sampling.
questions.lead_in: How should this tumor be classified within the ovarian tumor groups?
questions.stem: How should this tumor be classified within the ovarian tumor groups?
options: A specialized, monodermal teratoma, a type of germ cell tumor
A dysgerminoma analogous to seminoma
A sex cord stromal tumor that is feminizing
An immature teratoma with primitive neuroepithelium
A metastatic signet ring tumor from the stomach
choice_rationales: Germ cell tumors that differentiate along one line include struma ovarii as a monodermal teratoma.
Dysgerminoma shows sheets of large primitive cells with lymphoid septa.
Sex cord stromal tumors such as granulosa cell tumor are composed of stroma and sex cord elements.
Immature teratoma shows primitive neuroepithelial tissue, which was not found.
Krukenberg tumors are metastatic and bilateral in about 70 percent, which does not fit a thyroid only mass.
questions.explanation: Step 1. A tumor made almost entirely of thyroid follicles is struma ovarii. Step 2. The lecture places it among teratomas, which are germ cell tumors, as a specialized monodermal type that contains only thyroid elements. A related variant, strumal carcinoid, contains thyroid tissue and carcinoid tissue. A single tissue type does not make it a sex cord tumor.
visual_clues: Trace several epithelial rims. The pink material is luminal across multiple follicles.

questions.visual_target: Mature cartilage as a separate ovarian tissue pattern
questions.scenario: A 24-year-old woman has an incidental 8 cm right ovarian cystic mass. A section from a different teaching specimen of this kind shows isolated chondrocytes in lacunae within a broad matrix, along with skin elements.
questions.lead_in: What does this well differentiated cartilage imply about the tumor's behavior?
questions.stem: What does this well differentiated cartilage imply about the tumor's behavior?
options: It supports a Krukenberg tumor from a gastrointestinal primary
It supports an immature teratoma that needs prophylactic chemotherapy
It supports a dysgerminoma that is responsive to chemotherapy
It supports a mature cystic teratoma, which is benign in more than 90 percent of teratomas
It supports a granulosa cell tumor with estrogen secretion
choice_rationales: Krukenberg tumors have signet ring cells and a gastrointestinal primary.
Immature teratoma requires primitive tissue such as neuroepithelium, not mature cartilage.
Dysgerminoma is a sheet like proliferation of large primitive cells.
Mature, well differentiated tissue is the hallmark of the benign mature cystic teratoma.
Granulosa cell tumors are sex cord stromal tumors with Call-Exner bodies.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Mature cartilage with chondrocytes in lacunae, combined with skin elements, shows differentiation into multiple tissues, which is a mature cystic teratoma. Step 2. The lecture states that more than 90 percent of teratomas are benign mature cystic teratomas. Malignant transformation is rare and usually to squamous cell carcinoma, whereas immature teratomas contain primitive tissue such as neuroepithelium.
visual_clues: Rounded cells lie in lacunae in a continuous matrix.

questions.condition_overview: Mature cystic teratoma is the most common ovarian germ cell tumor and is benign. It is a unilocular cyst lined by skin with sebaceous glands and hair follicles, containing hair and greasy sebum and often teeth, bone, cartilage, thyroid, and brain tissue derived from all three germ layers. It is a frequent cause of adnexal masses in young women, is bilateral in about 10 to 15 percent, and can cause torsion or, rarely, autoimmune anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. A rare complication is malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma. Imaging shows fat that loses signal on fat suppression.

questions.tested_concept: Which complication would be most likely in the older patient?
questions.visual_target: Gross cavity and squamous lining in a separate ovarian specimen
questions.scenario: A 29-year-old woman has a pelvic mass. At surgery a right ovarian cyst is opened. The cavity is lined by a stratified squamous epithelium, with sebaceous secretion inside. Years later, a 60-year-old woman with an untreated lesion of this type develops a mass in the wall.
questions.lead_in: Which complication would be most likely in the older patient?
questions.stem: Which complication would be most likely in the older patient?
options: Transformation to a dysgerminoma
Spontaneous progression to extramammary Paget disease
Conversion to a granulosa cell tumor
Development of a Krukenberg tumor
Malignant transformation, usually to squamous cell carcinoma
choice_rationales: Dysgerminoma is a separate pure germ cell tumor.
Paget disease is a vulvar intraepidermal lesion.
Granulosa cell tumors are sex cord stromal tumors and are a different lineage.
Krukenberg tumors are metastases and do not arise from a dermoid cyst.
Malignant change in a dermoid cyst is usually squamous cell carcinoma, arising from the squamous lining.
questions.explanation: Step 1. A cyst lined by stratified squamous epithelium with sebaceous secretion is a mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst), about 90 percent unilateral and more often on the right. Step 2. The lecture notes that malignant transformation can occur and is usually to squamous cell carcinoma, which would be suspected when a mass develops in the wall of a long standing lesion.
visual_clues: A grossly open cavity is paired with a stratified squamous lining.

questions.scenario: A 17-year-old woman has a rapidly growing pelvic mass and a serum alpha fetoprotein of 2,400. A section from the tumor shows a vascular core wrapped by tumor cells that projects into a space.
questions.lead_in: Which tumor does this structure indicate, and how does the AFP result fit?

Granulosa cell tumor, whose Call-Exner bodies produce alpha fetoprotein
Mature cystic teratoma, whose chondrocytes produce alpha fetoprotein
Yolk sac tumor, whose cells produce alpha fetoprotein and form Schiller-Duval bodies
Dysgerminoma, whose cells produce alpha fetoprotein in fibrous septa

Granulosa cell tumors are marked by inhibin, not AFP.

The lecture lists elevated alpha fetoprotein as the laboratory finding and alpha fetoprotein positivity on immunostains, with hyaline PAS positive bodies containing AFP. The tumor is a germ cell tumor of young women and children.

Follow the rim of tumor around the vessel and the space outside that rim.

questions.condition_overview: Yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumor is a malignant germ cell tumor, the most common testicular tumor in infants and children, and it occurs in young women in the ovary. Microscopically a loose reticular or lacelike pattern of cuboidal cells surrounds open spaces. Schiller-Duval bodies are glomerulus-like structures with a central vessel surrounded by tumor cells within a space, and eosinophilic hyaline globules are common. Tumor cells secrete alpha-fetoprotein, which is a serum marker. It is chemosensitive.

questions.scenario: A 22-year-old woman has a large pelvic mass. Her serum AFP is high and hCG is normal. Immunostains on the tumor are positive for alpha fetoprotein, glypican 3, SALL4, and cytokeratin.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnosis is supported, and which marker would instead point to embryonal carcinoma?
questions.stem: Which diagnosis is supported, and which marker would instead point to embryonal carcinoma?
options: Dysgerminoma, whereas embryonal carcinoma is characterized by inhibin positivity
Struma ovarii, whereas embryonal carcinoma is characterized by thyroglobulin positivity
Yolk sac tumor, whereas embryonal carcinoma is characterized by CD30 and OCT3/4 positivity
Immature teratoma, whereas embryonal carcinoma is characterized by calponin positivity
Granulosa cell tumor, whereas embryonal carcinoma is characterized by AFP positivity
choice_rationales: Dysgerminoma does not stain for AFP, and inhibin is a granulosa marker.
Struma ovarii is thyroid tissue and does not have these germ cell markers.
Yolk sac tumor is AFP and glypican 3 positive, and embryonal carcinoma is CD30 and OCT3/4 positive.
Immature teratoma is defined by primitive tissue and calponin marks myoepithelium.
Granulosa cell tumor is inhibin positive and is not the AFP tumor described here.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Positivity for AFP, glypican 3, SALL4, and cytokeratin in a germ cell tumor with high AFP is a yolk sac tumor. Step 2. The lecture lists embryonal carcinoma with keratin, CD30, OCT3/4, NANOG, SALL4, and SOX2 positivity, so CD30 and OCT3/4 help separate it from yolk sac tumor, which is AFP and glypican 3 positive.

questions.scenario: A pathologist examines a yolk sac tumor and is surprised to see a loose reticular network around irregular spaces in one area and solid sheets and glandular areas in another.
questions.lead_in: What explains the variety of architectural patterns in the same tumor?
questions.stem: What explains the variety of architectural patterns in the same tumor?
options: The patterns recapitulate stages of yolk sac development, including reticular, myxoid, solid, glandular, and polyvesicular forms
Epidermal invasion has occurred, producing a mixed squamous tumor
The tumor is a metastatic signet ring tumor with variable mucin
The tumor has transformed into a granulosa cell tumor with Call-Exner bodies
Different tumors have collided, because yolk sac tumors never show more than one pattern
choice_rationales: The lecture lists multiple patterns that mirror yolk sac development.
Yolk sac tumors are germ cell tumors and are not squamous epithelial lesions.
Signet ring cells have intracellular mucin vacuoles and a gastrointestinal primary.
Granulosa tumors are sex cord stromal tumors, and one tumor type does not convert into another here.
The lecture describes a range of patterns in a single yolk sac tumor, not collision of separate tumors.
questions.explanation: Step 1. A loose reticular network with irregular spaces is one pattern of yolk sac tumor. Step 2. questions.condition_overview: Yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumor is a malignant germ cell tumor, the most common testicular tumor in infants and children, and it occurs in young women in the ovary. questions.condition_overview: Dysgerminoma is the ovarian counterpart of testicular seminoma and the most common malignant ovarian germ cell tumor, typically in young women. It forms a solid, pale, fleshy, lobulated mass. Microscopically large round cells with clear cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, and central nuclei with prominent nucleoli are arranged in nests separated by fibrous septa infiltrated by lymphocytes. Cells are OCT3/4, CD117, and PLAP positive. Tumors are highly radiosensitive and chemosensitive with an excellent prognosis. It can occur in gonadal dysgenesis, such as Swyer syndrome.

questions.condition_overview: A partial hydatidiform mole is usually triploid (69,XXY), from fertilization of one egg by two sperm, and an embryo or fetal parts are often present. It is graded by tubule formation, nuclear grade, and mitotic rate, and receptor status (ER, PR, HER2) guides therapy. It spreads to axillary nodes, bone, lung, liver, and brain.

choice_rationales: The conspicuous small cells wrap around the structure instead of replacing it. This choice describes invasive ductal carcinoma.

Mucinous carcinoma contains tumor clusters in extracellular mucin. The small invasive lobular carcinoma cells here wrap concentrically around a preexisting structure. This choice describes mucinous carcinoma.
The small cells lie around the structure rather than projecting into a lumen. This choice describes an intraductal papilloma.

Small tumor cells curve around the structure in successive rows. This targetoid relationship is an additional growth pattern beyond straight files. This choice describes lobular carcinoma in situ or invasive lobular carcinoma (targetoid pattern), which is what the image shows.
questions.explanation: Small tumor cells curve around the structure in successive rows. This targetoid relationship is an additional growth pattern beyond straight files. Mucinous carcinoma contains tumor clusters in extracellular mucin. The small invasive lobular carcinoma cells here wrap concentrically around a preexisting structure.

questions.condition_overview: Invasive lobular carcinoma is the second most common breast cancer. Small, discohesive cells with intracytoplasmic mucin infiltrate in single files (Indian files) and targetoid patterns around normal ducts, often without a discrete mass, and it can be missed on imaging. It is caused by loss of E-cadherin, so the cells are E-cadherin negative. It is frequently ER positive and often bilateral or multifocal, and it metastasizes to unusual sites such as the peritoneum, gastrointestinal tract, and ovaries.

questions.scenario: A 62-year-old woman has severe vulvar itching. Examination shows thin white patches on the vulva and perineum. A biopsy shows a thin epidermis with hyperkeratosis over a pale, sclerotic superficial dermis with a band of lymphocytes beneath.
questions.lead_in: What long-term risk should she be counseled about?
questions.stem: What long-term risk should she be counseled about?
options: Certain progression to invasive Paget disease
Direct transformation to adenocarcinoma of sweat glands
No risk, since the condition is purely cosmetic
A slightly increased chance of developing squamous cell carcinoma, although the lesion itself is not premalignant
Development of HPV related condylomata
choice_rationales: Paget disease is a separate intraepithelial glandular lesion and does not follow lichen sclerosus.
The related cancer is squamous, not a sweat gland adenocarcinoma.
The condition is associated with a modest cancer risk and symptoms, so it is not merely cosmetic.
The lecture states a slightly increased chance of squamous cell carcinoma.
Condylomata are HPV related and are not a consequence of sclerosis.
questions.explanation: Step 1. A thin epidermis over superficial dermal sclerosis with a lymphocytic band is lichen sclerosus. Step 2. The lecture says it is not premalignant but confers a slightly increased chance of developing squamous cell carcinoma, which is also why it is listed alongside differentiated VIN. Scratching can lead to ulceration, so follow up is warranted.
visual_clues: Follow the tissue from the surface into the pale zone below it.

questions.condition_overview: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic, probably autoimmune inflammatory skin disorder that mainly affects the vulva and perianal skin of postmenopausal women and also the penis (balanitis xerotica obliterans). Patients have intense itching and white, thin, parchment-like plaques that cause architectural change such as loss of labia minora and a narrowed introitus. Microscopically the epidermis is thin with loss of rete ridges, the superficial dermis is pale and homogenized (sclerotic), and a band of lymphocytes lies beneath it. It carries a small increased risk of vulvar squamous cell carcinoma, so persistent or ulcerated areas are biopsied. First-line therapy is a potent topical corticosteroid.

Large pale mucin positive cells, caused by sweat gland neoplasia
Acanthosis with long rete ridges and no atypia, caused by chronic scratching
Perinuclear halos in upper squamous cells, caused by HPV
Thin epidermis over dermal sclerosis with a lymphocytic band, with autoimmunity possibly playing a role
choice_rationales: A dermal papillary gland nodule describes papillary hidradenoma.
Mucin positive pale cells describe Paget disease.
Acanthosis describes squamous hyperplasia, a different pruritic plaque.
Koilocytes describe condyloma acuminatum from HPV.
Epidermal thinning with sclerosis and a T cell band fits, with possible autoimmunity.
questions.explanation: Step 1. White thinned patches with fusion of the labia and introital stenosis in a postmenopausal woman describe lichen sclerosus. Step 2. The lecture says etiology is unknown but autoimmunity may play a role, with thinning of the epidermis, basal cell degeneration, hyperkeratosis, superficial dermal sclerosis, and a lymphocytic band of activated T cells. The scarring explains the stenosis and dyspareunia.
visual_clues: The abnormality spans the superficial dermis beneath the thin surface.

Plasma cells filling the epidermis
A band of lymphocytes, representing activated T cells, along the deeper border of the pale zone
Eosinophils scattered through the epithelium
Fungal organisms in the stratum corneum

A colleague asks how this differs from her neighbor's lichen sclerosus and what precaution is needed.
questions.lead_in: What is the best interpretation of this biopsy and the precaution?
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation of this biopsy and the precaution?
options: Squamous hyperplasia (lichen simplex chronicus), benign but it may be seen next to invasive squamous cancer, so adjacent skin should be examined
Condyloma acuminatum, which is treated by wide excision for Paget cells
Differentiated VIN, which is always HPV positive
Lichen sclerosus, which is premalignant and needs immediate excision
Extramammary Paget disease, which is confirmed with a mucin stain
choice_rationales: Acanthosis and hyperkeratosis without atypia is squamous hyperplasia, and the neighboring cancer caution applies.
Condyloma shows exophytic papillary architecture and is not treated for Paget cells.
Differentiated VIN has basal atypia and is HPV negative.
Lichen sclerosus is thin and sclerotic, and it is not premalignant.
Paget disease has large pale mucin positive cells in the epidermis.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Broad thickening with hyperkeratosis and no atypia is squamous hyperplasia, also called lichen simplex chronicus, with leathery scaly plaques and pruritus. Step 2. The lecture states it is benign but may be seen next to invasive squamous cell cancer, so the clinician should confirm that no carcinoma is present in neighboring tissue. Lichen sclerosus differs by a thin epidermis and dermal sclerosis.
visual_clues: The expanded squamous layer sends elongated ridges down toward the dermis.

questions.condition_overview: Squamous hyperplasia (lichen simplex chronicus) is a benign thickening of vulvar epidermis from chronic rubbing and scratching, producing white, leathery plaques with acanthosis and hyperkeratosis without atypia. Intense pruritus is typical, and treatment involves high-potency topical corticosteroids and breaking the itch-scratch cycle. Biopsy of persistent lesions excludes lichen sclerosus and vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia.

questions.scenario: A 24-year-old woman has several raised, rough papules around the vulva. A biopsy shows squamous cells in the upper layers with enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei with irregular membranes, some multinucleation, and perinuclear clearing.
questions.lead_in: What do these cells indicate about the cause of her lesions?
questions.stem: What do these cells indicate about the cause of her lesions?
options: Fungal infection, since halos mark hyphae
Autoimmune basal cell damage, since koilocytes form in lichen sclerosus
Apocrine neoplasia, since clearing marks myoepithelium
Syphilis, since perinuclear halos are specific to condyloma latum
Productive HPV infection, since koilocytes reflect viral cytopathic effect
choice_rationales: Fungal organisms are shown by PAS, not by perinuclear halos.
Lichen sclerosus features basal cell degeneration and dermal sclerosis, not koilocytes.
Apocrine neoplasia forms dermal glands, not halo cells in the squamous epithelium.
Condyloma latum is the syphilis lesion and is separate from HPV related koilocytic change.
Koilocytes are the cytopathic effect of productive HPV infection.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia, irregular membranes, multinucleation, and perinuclear cytoplasmic vacuolization are koilocytes. Step 2. The lecture calls these viral cytopathic effects that characterize productive HPV infection, as in condyloma acuminatum. They help separate it from condyloma latum of syphilis.
visual_clues: Inspect several nuclei next to the surface keratin.

questions.condition_overview: Condyloma acuminatum is a benign, exophytic anogenital wart caused by low-risk human papillomavirus (mainly types 6 and 11). It appears as single or multiple raised, rough, cauliflower-like papules. Microscopically there are papillary fronds of acanthotic squamous epithelium over fibrovascular cores, with hyperkeratosis and koilocytes (cells with enlarged wrinkled nuclei and perinuclear clearing) in the upper layers. Condylomata are transmitted sexually, are not generally premalignant, and are treated by ablation, topical therapy, or excision. HPV vaccination prevents most cases.

questions.scenario: A 26-year-old woman has multiple raised vulvar growths. Biopsy shows finger-like, tree-like cores of stroma covered by thickened squamous epithelium with koilocytic change. Her partner asks whether this could be syphilis.
questions.lead_in: Which statement correctly distinguishes this lesion?
questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes this lesion?
options: It is Paget disease with intracytoplasmic mucin
It is a papillary hidradenoma arising from apocrine glands
It is condyloma latum caused by HPV, whereas condyloma acuminatum is the syphilitic lesion
It is condyloma acuminatum caused by HPV, whereas condyloma latum is the syphilitic lesion
It is a premalignant lesion of differentiated VIN with p53 mutation
choice_rationales: Paget disease is an intraepidermal glandular process.
Hidradenoma is a dermal apocrine nodule that does not connect to the epidermis.
The names are reversed in this option.
Acuminatum is HPV related and latum is syphilitic, matching the lecture.
Differentiated VIN shows basal atypia and is not exophytic with koilocytes.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Papillary exophytic tree like stromal cores covered by thickened squamous epithelium with koilocytes is condyloma acuminatum. Step 2. The lecture lists two benign exophytic condylomas, acuminatum from HPV and latum from syphilis, and the koilocytic change identifies the HPV form. Penile, urethral, and perianal condylomata also occur.
visual_clues: The decisive changes are perinuclear and occur in differentiated squamous cells.

questions.condition_overview: Differentiated VIN is an HPV-independent precancer of the vulva that occurs in older women and is typically associated with lichen sclerosus or lichen planus. The atypia is confined to the basal and parabasal layers, with premature keratinization and maturing, eosinophilic superficial cells that make it easy to overlook. Mutated p53 is often present. dVIN is the usual precursor of HPV-independent keratinizing vulvar squamous cell carcinoma and progresses rapidly, so it is excised.

questions.explanation: Step 1. A small circumscribed dermal nodule with complex papillary glands arising in the interlabial sulcus is papillary hidradenoma of apocrine origin. Step 2. The lecture notes mitoses may be brisk, but benign features are the sharp circumscription, an intact myoepithelial layer, normal skin cover, and no connection to the epidermis. Surface bleeding or ulceration can mimic carcinoma clinically.

questions.condition_overview: Papillary hidradenoma is a benign tumor of the anogenital (mammary-like) sweat glands that forms a small, well-circumscribed, often asymptomatic nodule in the dermis of the vulva. Microscopically it shows branching papillary and tubular glands lined by two cell layers, an inner luminal layer and an outer myoepithelial layer (highlighted by calponin or p63), within a fibrous stroma. It resembles intraductal papilloma of the breast and can be mistaken for adenocarcinoma, but it is benign and cured by excision.

questions.condition_overview: Papillary hidradenoma is a benign tumor of the anogenital (mammary-like) sweat glands that forms a small, well-circumscribed, often asymptomatic nodule in the dermis of the vulva. Microscopically it shows branching papillary and tubular glands lined by two cell layers, an inner luminal layer and an outer myoepithelial layer (highlighted by calponin or p63), within a fibrous stroma. It resembles intraductal papilloma of the breast and can be mistaken for adenocarcinoma, but it is benign and cured by excision.

questions.condition_overview: Condyloma acuminatum is a benign, exophytic anogenital wart caused by low-risk human papillomavirus (mainly types 6 and 11). It appears as single or multiple raised, rough, cauliflower-like papules. Microscopically there are papillary fronds of acanthotic squamous epithelium over fibrovascular cores, with hyperkeratosis and koilocytes (cells with enlarged wrinkled nuclei and perinuclear clearing) in the upper layers. Condylomata are transmitted sexually, are not generally premalignant, and are treated by ablation, topical therapy, or excision. HPV vaccination prevents most cases.

questions.condition_overview: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is HPV-driven dysplasia of the cervical squamous epithelium graded by the depth of epithelium replaced by atypical cells (CIN 1 lower third, CIN 2 two thirds, CIN 3 full thickness). At colposcopy, application of acetic acid whitens areas with dense nuclear protein (acetowhite epithelium) because of a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. Lugol iodine fails to stain dysplastic cells because they lack glycogen, giving a mustard-yellow area. These findings guide biopsy. Higher grades are treated by excision or ablation to prevent invasive carcinoma.

It is Paget disease, and vaccines protect against it
It is LSIL, and HPV 16 and 18 are never involved
It is HSIL (CIN III), and HPV vaccines protect against types 16 and 18 but cannot treat established infection
It is invasive carcinoma, since the surface is involved
choice_rationales: CIN I is LSIL and is limited to the lower third.
Paget disease is vulvar and is unrelated to HPV vaccination.
HPV 16 and 18 account for about half of HSIL.
CIN III is HSIL, and vaccines prevent but do not treat established infection.
Invasive carcinoma requires invasion into the underlying stroma.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Full thickness atypia with no maturation is HSIL (CIN III). Step 2. The lecture states HPV types 16 and 18 account for about half of HSILs, and that vaccines made of L1 capsid protein protect against these types but cannot protect against established infections, so screening continues. Invasion needs stromal penetration, not surface involvement alone.

questions.condition_overview: High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL, CIN 2 and CIN 3) is the true cervical precancer. It arises from persistent infection with high-risk HPV (types 16 and 18 most often), in which viral E6 and E7 proteins inactivate p53 and Rb. Immature basaloid cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, hyperchromatic nuclei, and mitoses occupy at least the lower two thirds up to the full thickness of the epithelium, with loss of maturation toward the surface. Diffuse strong p16 staining supports the diagnosis. HSIL is treated by excision or ablation because it can progress to invasive squamous cell carcinoma.

Cervical condyloma is exophytic and not the CIN spectrum shown.

Atypia beyond the lower third is not normal.

The lecture merges CIN II and CIN III into HSIL, which has about 60 percent persistence and about 10 percent progression to carcinoma, compared with the mostly regressing LSIL. Neither panel shows stromal invasion.
visual_clues: In the second panel the surface retains greater maturation.

questions.condition_overview: Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL, CIN 1) is a productive HPV infection of the cervical squamous epithelium. Atypical cells with koilocytic change are confined mainly to the lower third of the epithelium, and the upper layers mature normally. It most often reflects low- or high-risk HPV, usually regresses spontaneously, especially in young women, and is generally followed rather than treated aggressively. On Pap smear the finding is koilocytes with mildly enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei in superficial and intermediate cells.

questions.condition_overview: Adenomyosis is the presence of benign endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, deeper than the usual endometrial-myometrial junction. The uterus enlarges symmetrically and has a thickened, trabeculated wall with small cystic or hemorrhagic foci. Patients have heavy, painful menses and a boggy, tender uterus. Microscopically there are islands of endometrial-type glands with stromal cuffs among smooth muscle bundles, with hypertrophy of the surrounding muscle. On MRI it thickens the junctional zone. Definitive treatment is hysterectomy.

questions.condition_overview: Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) are benign smooth muscle tumors and the most common tumor in women, growth being estrogen and progesterone dependent. They are classified as submucosal (beneath the endometrium, causing the most bleeding), intramural (within the wall), or subserosal (beneath the serosa, causing pressure effects). They are well-circumscribed, firm, whorled, white-tan masses with interlacing bundles of uniform spindle cells without atypia. Symptoms include heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure, and infertility, and they shrink after menopause. Malignant transformation (leiomyosarcoma) is rare.

questions.condition_overview: Endometriosis is the presence of functional endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus, most often on the ovaries, pelvic peritoneum, and rectovaginal septum, and rarely in the bladder, vagina, or even the lung. Ectopic tissue responds to cyclic hormones, bleeds, and causes chronic inflammation and fibrosis. Patients have dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain, dyspareunia, and infertility. Ovarian involvement forms endometriomas (chocolate cysts) filled with old blood. Microscopically two of three elements are needed: endometrial glands, stroma, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages. Catamenial symptoms, such as thoracic or bladder symptoms with menses, suggest distant implants.

Excellent prognosis with no follow up needed because it is a benign dermoid cyst
choice_rationales: Stage I tumors carry an excellent prognosis, not a poor one in all cases.
Stage I immature teratoma has an excellent prognosis with prophylactic chemotherapy and early recurrences.
This tumor is not an estrogen secreting tumor.
Dysgerminoma is the tumor that is highly responsive to chemotherapy, and teratoma is treated differently.
A mature dermoid cyst is cystic and benign, which does not match primitive tissue.

The lecture states stage I tumors have an excellent prognosis, treatment is prophylactic chemotherapy, most recurrences occur within the first 2 years, and absence of disease beyond that period gives an excellent chance of cure. Rapid growth and capsular penetration can occur.

questions.condition_overview: Immature teratoma is a malignant germ cell tumor of young women that contains immature, primitive tissue, most commonly neuroepithelium forming rosettes and tubules with crowded dark nuclei, along with mature elements such as cartilage and glands. It forms a bulky solid mass with hemorrhage and necrosis. Grade is determined by the amount of immature neuroepithelium, and it is treated with surgery and chemotherapy for higher grades.

questions.lead_in: Which pairing best distinguishes this teenager's tumor from her sister's?
questions.stem: Which pairing best distinguishes this teenager's tumor from her sister's?

Hers is a Krukenberg tumor and her sister's is a dysgerminoma
Hers is a yolk sac tumor and her sister's is a thecoma
Hers is a mature cystic teratoma and her sister's is an immature teratoma
Hers is a dysgerminoma and her sister's is a granulosa cell tumor
choice_rationales: Immature teratoma is solid with primitive tissue, while a mature cystic teratoma is cystic and benign.
Krukenberg tumors are metastatic and bilateral, which does not fit.
Yolk sac tumor is marked by AFP and Schiller-Duval bodies, not hair and cartilage.
The terms are reversed in this option.
The tissue types described are teratomas, not dysgerminoma and granulosa tumor.
questions.explanation: Step 1. A bulky, predominantly solid tumor with primitive tissue in an adolescent is an immature teratoma. Step 2. The lecture contrasts it with mature cystic teratomas, which are more than 90 percent of teratomas, usually cystic and benign. Immature teratomas have embryonal tissue, frequently neuroepithelium, grow rapidly, and may penetrate the capsule.

questions.condition_overview: Mature cystic teratoma is the most common ovarian germ cell tumor and is benign. It is a unilocular cyst lined by skin with sebaceous glands and hair follicles, containing hair and greasy sebum and often teeth, bone, cartilage, thyroid, and brain tissue derived from all three germ layers. It is a frequent cause of adnexal masses in young women, is bilateral in about 10 to 15 percent, and can cause torsion or, rarely, autoimmune anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. A rare complication is malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma. Imaging shows fat that loses signal on fat suppression.

Mucin secretion by a Krukenberg tumor

questions.condition_overview: Granulosa cell tumor is a sex cord-stromal tumor of the ovary that often secretes estrogen, causing precocious puberty in girls, or abnormal bleeding and endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma in older women. Microscopically small uniform cells with pale grooved (coffee-bean) nuclei form microfollicular patterns around Call-Exner bodies (small spaces with eosinophilic material), and tumor cells stain for inhibin and calretinin. Most are low grade and unilateral, but late recurrence can occur. Treatment is surgery.

Thecoma, with Meigs syndrome causing breast growth
Krukenberg tumor, with GI metastasis causing breast growth
Dysgerminoma, with chemotherapy response causing early puberty
Juvenile granulosa cell tumor, with estrogen causing precocious sexual development
choice_rationales: A mature teratoma does not secrete hormone that causes precocious puberty.
Meigs syndrome is ascites with right hydrothorax associated with fibroma, not this case.
Krukenberg tumors are adult metastases and do not occur this way in a child.
Dysgerminoma is a germ cell tumor, not an estrogenic tumor.
Estrogen from a juvenile granulosa cell tumor causes precocious sexual development.

questions.scenario: A 52-year-old woman with epigastric discomfort and weight loss has bilateral ovarian masses. A section shows pale tumor cells with large intracellular vacuoles that push the nuclei to the cell edge.
questions.lead_in: Where should the search for the primary tumor begin?
questions.stem: Where should the search for the primary tumor begin?
options: The vulvar skin, since the cells are Paget cells
The thyroid, since the vacuoles are colloid
The gastrointestinal tract, especially the stomach, since this signet ring pattern most often originates there
The germ cells of the other ovary, since they are teratoma components
The uterine myometrium, since the cells are endometrial
choice_rationales: Paget cells are vulvar, not ovarian metastases.
Thyroid follicles contain colloid, not signet ring vacuoles.
Krukenberg tumors most often come from a gastrointestinal primary, especially gastric.
A teratoma is a primary germ cell tumor, not a mucin rich metastasis.
Endometrial cells do not form this pattern in the lecture.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Mucin rich cells with intracellular vacuoles displacing the nucleus are signet ring cells, and bilateral ovarian involvement defines Krukenberg tumor. Step 2. The lecture states Krukenberg tumors are metastatic signet ring adenocarcinomas, from a gastrointestinal primary in about 70 percent of cases (gastric origin is typical), and can also arise from colon, breast, appendix, and biliary tract. Her epigastric symptoms point to the stomach.
visual_clues: Check whether the pale material lies inside a cell or in a shared lumen.

questions.condition_overview: Krukenberg tumor is a metastasis to the ovary, usually bilateral, from a mucin-producing adenocarcinoma, most often of the stomach, and also the colon or breast. The ovaries are enlarged and nodular. Microscopically, signet-ring cells with intracytoplasmic mucin displacing the nucleus infiltrate a cellular, reactive ovarian stroma, often with mucin pools. Prognosis is poor and depends on the primary site, and the finding of a bilateral solid ovarian mass should prompt a search for a gastrointestinal primary.

A primary sex cord tumor with Call-Exner bodies
A primary serous carcinoma with papillary growth
A metastatic signet ring cell adenocarcinoma (Krukenberg tumor), usually from a gastrointestinal primary, often bilateral

Call-Exner bodies define granulosa cell tumor.
Serous carcinoma is papillary and does not have intracellular mucin vacuoles.

Schiller-Duval bodies define yolk sac tumor, not signet ring cells.

Large intact follicles containing homogeneous colloid
Small cells infiltrating stroma in narrow files
Crowded primitive neural tubules within a solid nodule
Broad epithelial sheets around a central vascular stalk
choice_rationales: The conspicuous arrangement here is linear infiltration by small cells. This choice describes a signet-ring cell metastasis.
The cells traverse stroma rather than lining rounded follicles. This choice describes struma ovarii.

Small tumor cells infiltrate ovarian stroma in narrow linear files. The original field instead emphasizes individual cells with prominent cytoplasmic vacuoles. This choice describes metastatic lobular-type carcinoma (single-file infiltration), which is what the image shows.
The lesional cells follow thin stromal tracks rather than forming tubules. This choice describes immature teratoma.
The epithelial component lies in slender files without a central stalk. This choice describes yolk sac tumor.
questions.explanation: Small tumor cells infiltrate ovarian stroma in narrow linear files. The original field instead emphasizes individual cells with prominent cytoplasmic vacuoles. The epithelial component lies in slender files without a central stalk.

questions.scenario: A 58-year-old woman with recurrent E. coli urinary tract infections has soft yellow plaques on cystoscopy. A biopsy shows foamy histiocytes containing rounded, dense, laminated inclusions at the two arrows.
questions.lead_in: What do these inclusions represent, and what failure in the macrophages produces them?
questions.stem: What do these inclusions represent, and what failure in the macrophages produces them?
options: Schiller-Duval bodies, papillations from yolk sac differentiation
Michaelis-Gutmann bodies, mineralized remnants of partially digested bacteria caused by insufficient bacterial killing
Koilocytes, enlarged nuclei with halos from HPV
Signet ring vacuoles, mucin displacing nuclei
Call-Exner bodies, follicle like structures in granulosa cells
choice_rationales: Schiller-Duval bodies are yolk sac tumor structures in the ovary.
Michaelis-Gutmann bodies are mineralized debris in macrophages with defective bacterial killing.
Koilocytes are squamous cells showing HPV effect.
Signet ring cells are tumor cells in Krukenberg tumor.
Call-Exner bodies are found in granulosa cell tumors.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Foamy histiocytes with basophilic, laminated, mineralized inclusions are Michaelis-Gutmann bodies, the hallmark of malakoplakia. Step 2. The lecture explains the pathogenesis as insufficient killing of bacteria by macrophages, so partially digested bacteria accumulate with deposition of iron and calcium. This explains the link with chronic bacterial infection.
visual_clues: Trace the arrows to the rounded dense bodies among the pink cells.

questions.condition_overview: Malakoplakia is a chronic inflammatory condition, most often of the bladder, caused by defective bacterial killing by macrophages, usually with Escherichia coli infection. Soft yellow-tan plaques form on the mucosa. Microscopically sheets of foamy, granular histiocytes (von Hansemann cells) contain round, targetoid, laminated, calcified Michaelis-Gutmann bodies. It is treated with antibiotics that penetrate macrophages.

Chronic cystitis, treated by catheter removal
Endometriosis of the bladder, treated with hormones
Invasive urothelial carcinoma, treated with BCG
Malakoplakia, an inflammatory condition, treated with antibiotics
choice_rationales: Flat carcinoma in situ shows high grade atypia of the urothelium.
Chronic cystitis shows chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and metaplasia without Michaelis-Gutmann bodies.
Bladder endometriosis contains endometrial glands, stroma, and hemosiderin laden macrophages.
Invasive urothelial carcinoma shows tumor nests and cords in the wall, not histiocytes.
The lecture identifies malakoplakia as an inflammatory condition treated with antibiotics.

Soft plaques with foamy histiocytes and Michaelis-Gutmann bodies in a patient with infection is malakoplakia, a rare chronic inflammatory condition that is not neoplastic. Step 2. The lecture lists antibiotics as the treatment, consistent with its link to inadequate bacterial killing. It most commonly affects the bladder but can occur in other organs.

questions.lead_in: Why does this gross pattern direct the biopsy, and what is expected histologically?
questions.stem: Why does this gross pattern direct the biopsy, and what is expected histologically?
options: Plaques are typical of schistosomiasis, expected to show only squamous carcinoma
Plaques are typical of papillary urothelial carcinoma, expected to show fibrovascular fronds
Pale plaques are typical of squamous hyperplasia, expected to show glycogen rich cells
Soft yellow plaques are typical of malakoplakia, expected to show foamy histiocytes with Michaelis-Gutmann bodies
Plaques are typical of CIS, expected to show cohesive normal urothelium
choice_rationales: Schistosomiasis is a risk factor for squamous carcinoma and does not describe these histiocytes.
Papillary carcinoma forms projecting fronds, not flat plaques.
Squamous hyperplasia is a vulvar lesion and is not what the lecture describes here.
Soft plaques with foamy histiocytes and Michaelis-Gutmann bodies fit malakoplakia.
Carcinoma in situ is velvety and poorly cohesive, not a plaque with histiocytes.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Papules, plaques, or ulceration of the bladder mucosa, originally described as soft yellowish plaques, fit malakoplakia. Step 2. Histology shows foamy histiocytes with Michaelis-Gutmann bodies. questions.condition_overview: Seminoma is the most common testicular germ cell tumor, in men aged 15 to 45. It forms a homogeneous, pale tan-white, fleshy, bulging mass. Microscopically sheets or nests of uniform large cells with clear glycogen-rich cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, and round central nuclei with prominent nucleoli are separated by fibrous septa with lymphocytes. Cells express OCT3/4, CD117, and PLAP. It is highly radiosensitive and has an excellent prognosis, and it commonly arises in undescended testes.

questions.scenario: A pathologist reviews the testicular mass from the cryptorchid patient. The slide shows nests of large pale cells separated by fibrous septa containing abundant lymphocytes, with an occasional granuloma. The surgeon asks which tumor in the ovary is analogous.
questions.lead_in: Which combination fits, and what is the ovarian analog?
questions.stem: Which combination fits, and what is the ovarian analog?
options: Seminoma, analogous to ovarian dysgerminoma, with nests of large clear cells and lymphocyte rich septa
Choriocarcinoma, analogous to ovarian thecoma, with spindle cells
Embryonal carcinoma, analogous to ovarian yolk sac tumor, with papillary growth and necrosis
Yolk sac tumor, analogous to ovarian granulosa cell tumor, with Call-Exner bodies
Teratoma, analogous to ovarian Krukenberg tumor, with signet ring cells
choice_rationales: Seminoma and dysgerminoma share nests of large clear cells and lymphoid septa.
Choriocarcinoma has trophoblastic cells, not lymphoid septa.
Embryonal carcinoma has papillary growth and necrosis, not lymphoid septa.
Yolk sac tumor is not analogous to a sex cord tumor.
Teratoma contains mixed differentiated tissue and Krukenberg tumors are metastases.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Large clear cells in nests separated by lymphocyte rich fibrous septa, sometimes with granulomas, are seminoma. Step 2. The lecture equates seminoma with ovarian dysgerminoma, which has the same histology and is radiosensitive. Embryonal carcinoma shows solid, glandular, and papillary growth with anaplastic cells and necrosis.
visual_clues: Compare the large pale cells in nests with the small dark cells in the bands.

questions.lead_in: Which diagnosis does this integrate, and how can a mild hCG rise be explained?
questions.stem: Which diagnosis does this integrate, and how can a mild hCG rise be explained?
options: Seminoma, in which syncytiotrophoblasts are present in about 15 percent of cases and can raise hCG
Spermatocytic tumor, since it is OCT3/4 positive
Sertoli cell tumor, since it is CD117 positive
Choriocarcinoma, since hCG elevation always means choriocarcinoma
Yolk sac tumor, since OCT3/4 marks yolk sac cells
choice_rationales: Seminoma can contain syncytiotrophoblasts that raise hCG modestly.
Spermatocytic tumor is OCT3/4 negative and lacks lymphocytes.
Sertoli cell tumors are sex cord tumors and do not match germ cell markers.
Choriocarcinoma needs trophoblastic tumor morphology, and hCG alone is not diagnostic.
Yolk sac tumor is AFP positive, not OCT3/4 positive.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Nests of large cells with lymphocytes and OCT3/4 and CD117 positivity are a seminoma. Step 2. The lecture states that beta hCG positivity occurs in about 15 percent of cases from syncytiotrophoblasts, so a mild hCG rise does not by itself change the diagnosis. Spermatocytic tumor is distinct, being CD117 and SALL4 positive but PLAP and OCT3/4 negative, with no lymphocytes, granulomas, or GCNIS.
visual_clues: The dark lymphocytes cluster in the septa, between the pale tumor nests.

options: Grooved oval nuclei with small follicle like structures
Spindle cells with central nuclei in whorls
Distinct cell borders with clear cytoplasm and large central nuclei with prominent nucleoli
Indistinct borders with vacuolated cytoplasm pushing the nucleus aside
Small dark cells with scant cytoplasm and no nucleoli
choice_rationales: Grooved nuclei with follicles describe granulosa cell tumor.
Spindle cells in whorls describe a stromal tumor.
Distinct borders with large central nuclei and prominent nucleoli describe seminoma cells.
Peripheral nuclei in vacuolated cells describe signet ring cells.
Small dark cells with scant cytoplasm do not match the large clear cells.
questions.explanation: Step 1. The lecture describes seminoma cells as having distinct membranes, clear or light cytoplasm, and a large central nucleus with a prominent nucleolus, arranged in nests divided by fibrous bands with lymphocytes. Step 2. Signet ring cells have peripheral nuclei, spindle cells with central nuclei describe thecoma or fibroma, and grooved nuclei with follicles describe granulosa cell tumor, so the cytology separates seminoma from these.
visual_clues: The large cells have distinct outlines and centrally located round nuclei.

questions.scenario: A 24-year-old man has a rapidly growing testicular mass with elevated markers and lung nodules. The cut surface of a separate specimen shows patchy dark and pale areas within a solid lobulated mass, with hemorrhage and necrosis.
questions.lead_in: Why does this gross pattern argue against a pure seminoma?
questions.stem: Why does this gross pattern argue against a pure seminoma?
options: Hemorrhage and necrosis are expected in seminoma, which is homogeneous only after fixation
Dark and pale areas show a benign spermatocytic tumor
Dark and pale areas show BPH nodules
Hemorrhage and necrosis suggest a nonseminomatous germ cell tumor such as embryonal carcinoma, which is more aggressive and often metastatic
Dark and pale areas show a benign Leydig cell tumor
choice_rationales: Hemorrhage and necrosis are rare in seminoma.
Spermatocytic tumor is distinct and is not the aggressive tumor described.
BPH is a prostate condition.
Variegated hemorrhagic, necrotic tumors favor nonseminomatous types such as embryonal carcinoma.
A Leydig cell tumor is a sex cord tumor and does not account for metastasis here.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Seminoma is a homogeneous, fleshy mass with rare hemorrhage and necrosis. Step 2. The lecture describes embryonal carcinoma as more aggressive than seminoma, often metastatic, with solid, glandular, and papillary growth, anaplastic cells, and necrosis. A variegated cut surface with hemorrhage and necrosis therefore favors a nonseminomatous or mixed germ cell tumor.
visual_clues: Irregular dark and pale areas interrupt the tan lobulated surface.

questions.scenario: A 28-year-old man with cryptorchidism has a testicular biopsy from tissue next to his tumor. The field shows large atypical cells lining a recognizable seminiferous tubule, with no invasion into the stroma. The cells stain for PLAP.
questions.lead_in: What does this boundary distinguish, and why does it matter?
questions.stem: What does this boundary distinguish, and why does it matter?
options: Invasive seminoma already spreading in the stroma
A benign Sertoli cell tumor
A spermatocytic tumor that is unrelated to GCNIS
Malakoplakia of the testis
Intratubular germ cell neoplasia (GCNIS) confined within a tubule, the precursor from which most germ cell tumors arise
choice_rationales: Invasive seminoma would extend into stroma, which is absent here.
Sertoli cell tumors are sex cord tumors and do not stain with PLAP.
Spermatocytic tumor is PLAP negative and unrelated to GCNIS.
Malakoplakia is a histiocytic condition of the urinary tract.
A tubule encircling atypical germ cells is intratubular germ cell neoplasia, the precursor lesion.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Large atypical cells confined within a recognizable seminiferous tubule and positive for PLAP are intratubular germ cell neoplasia (GCNIS). Step 2. The lecture states most germ cell tumors are preceded by intratubular germ cell neoplasia, and that cryptorchidism increases risk three to five times. PLAP stains germ cell tumors and intratubular neoplasia, whereas spermatocytic tumor is unrelated to GCNIS and is PLAP negative.
visual_clues: The large abnormal cells stay within the contour of a seminiferous tubule.

questions.condition_overview: Germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS) is the precursor lesion of most testicular germ cell tumors. Large atypical cells with clear cytoplasm, large nuclei, and prominent nucleoli line the base of seminiferous tubules next to the basement membrane, and they stain for PLAP, OCT3/4, and CD117. Risk factors include cryptorchidism and gonadal dysgenesis. It can progress to invasive tumors over years.

questions.visual_target: Which immunostain combination supports the tumor pattern in this field?
questions.stem: Which immunostain combination supports the tumor pattern in this field?
options: OCT3/4 and CD117
p63 and CK903
CD30 and AFP
HER2 and estrogen receptor
Calponin and SMA
choice_rationales: The pale tumor cells and lymphocyte-rich septa favor seminoma. R16 lists OCT3/4 and CD117 as useful markers for this pattern. This choice describes OCT3/4 and CD117 (seminoma markers), which is what the image shows.

p63 and CK903 assess prostatic basal cells in the PIN4 examples. The germ cell tumor pattern shown here is seminoma and calls for OCT3/4 and CD117. This choice describes p63 and CK903 (prostate basal markers).

The seminoma slide lists CD30 and AFP as negative. In the germ cell differential, CD30 can support embryonal carcinoma and AFP can support yolk sac differentiation. This choice describes CD30 and AFP (embryonal carcinoma and yolk sac tumor).
HER2 and estrogen receptor are breast carcinoma biomarkers in the quiz. OCT3/4 and CD117 instead fit the seminoma pattern here. This choice describes HER2 and estrogen receptor (breast markers).

Calponin and SMA assess myoepithelial or smooth muscle differentiation in other examples. They do not establish germ cell differentiation in this seminoma field. This choice describes calponin and SMA (myoepithelial markers).
questions.explanation: The pale tumor cells and lymphocyte-rich septa fit seminoma. R16 identifies OCT3/4 and CD117 as useful germ cell markers in that setting and describes CD30 and AFP as negative.
visual_clues: The pale tumor cells and lymphocyte-rich septa fit seminoma.

questions.lead_in: Which implantation site and complication risk does this suggest?
questions.stem: Which implantation site and complication risk does this suggest?
options: A placenta accreta of the uterine wall
A right tubal ectopic pregnancy, which can rupture at about 8 weeks with life threatening hemorrhage
An ovarian cyst that always resolves
A normal intrauterine pregnancy
A complete mole in the uterine cavity
choice_rationales: Placenta accreta involves the uterine wall and a placenta in the uterus.
A tubal implantation in a patient with prior PID can rupture at about 8 weeks.
An ovarian cyst does not explain a positive hCG with an empty uterus and a tubal abnormality.
A normal intrauterine pregnancy would be seen in the uterus.
A complete mole is intrauterine and would not mark a tubal site.
questions.explanation: Step 1. A positive hCG with an empty uterus and a marked abnormality in the tube indicates an ectopic pregnancy, and more than 95 percent occur in the fallopian tube. Step 2. The lecture lists risk factors that alter tube anatomy, including PID, salpingitis, and prior pelvic surgery, and states that continued growth dilates the tube and can rupture at about 8 weeks with possible life threatening hemorrhage. Other outcomes include spontaneous expulsion or involution.
visual_clues: Use the upper arrow as a tubal landmark and follow the lower arrow to its tip.

questions.condition_overview: An ectopic pregnancy is implantation outside the uterine cavity, most commonly in the fallopian tube (ampulla most often, then isthmus and fimbria), and less often in the interstitial portion, ovary, cervix, cesarean scar, or abdomen. Risk factors include prior pelvic inflammatory disease, tubal surgery, and previous ectopic pregnancy. Patients have pain, bleeding, and amenorrhea, and rupture can cause fatal hemorrhage. hCG rises more slowly than normal and ultrasound shows no intrauterine pregnancy. Treatment is methotrexate or surgery.

questions.scenario: A surgical diagram shows several marked sites along the fallopian tube and uterus where a pregnancy can implant. Two marks lie within the tube itself, clearly lateral to the uterine wall.
questions.lead_in: Which pair is drawn within the tube lateral to the uterine wall, and what does the lecture say about how often the tube is the site?
questions.stem: Which pair is drawn within the tube lateral to the uterine wall, and what does the lecture say about how often the tube is the site?
options: The ampullary and interstitial sites, and none are tubal
The isthmic and ampullary sites, and more than 95 percent of ectopic pregnancies are tubal
The abdominal and uterine sites, and all are tubal
The ovarian and cervical sites, and more than 95 percent are tubal
The interstitial and cornual sites, and 5 percent are tubal
choice_rationales: The interstitial site lies in the uterine wall, and the tube is the main site.
Isthmic and ampullary sites are within the tube and lateral to the uterine wall, and the tube accounts for over 95 percent.
Not all ectopic pregnancies are tubal, but more than 95 percent are.
Ovarian and cervical sites are not tubal segments, even though ectopic pregnancy can occur elsewhere rarely.
The interstitial segment lies in the uterine wall, and the tubal proportion is far higher than 5 percent.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Moving from the uterus outward, the tubal segments are the interstitial part within the uterine wall, then the isthmus, the ampulla, and the fimbriated end, so the isthmic and ampullary sites lie within the tube lateral to the uterine wall. Step 2. The lecture states that more than 95 percent of ectopic pregnancies occur in the fallopian tube, so tubal sites are the main concern. The segment naming is anatomical knowledge not detailed in the lecture text.
visual_clues: Trace the tube outward from where it meets the uterus.

The interstitial marker lies on the ovary, whereas the isthmic marker lies in the cavity

Both markers lie in the uterine wall
They cannot be distinguished at all
The tubal marker lies in the uterine cavity and the ovarian marker in the tube
The tubal marker follows the distal tube, whereas the ovarian marker lies within the ovary

questions.condition_overview: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a malignant proliferation of ductal epithelial cells confined by the basement membrane. Patterns include comedo (high grade with central necrosis and calcifications), solid, cribriform, and papillary. It is usually detected as mammographic microcalcifications. Left untreated, a proportion progresses to invasive ductal carcinoma. Treatment is lumpectomy with radiation, or mastectomy, and endocrine therapy if ER positive.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis best accounts for the arrangement in this section?
options: Lobular carcinoma in situ
Comedo type ductal carcinoma in situ
Invasive ductal carcinoma
Invasive lobular carcinoma
Mucinous carcinoma
choice_rationales: Lobular carcinoma in situ expands lobules with loosely cohesive cells. The necrotic central cores within expanded ducts favor comedo-type ductal carcinoma in situ. This choice describes lobular carcinoma in situ.

Central necrosis within expanded ducts rimmed by atypical epithelium is the characteristic pattern of comedo-type ductal carcinoma in situ. This choice describes comedo-type ductal carcinoma in situ, which is what the image shows.

Invasive ductal carcinoma would show irregular epithelial glands infiltrating desmoplastic stroma. The necrotic material here remains within expanded ducts. This choice describes invasive ductal carcinoma.
Invasive lobular carcinoma would show single files of discohesive cells in stroma. This field instead shows intraductal necrosis. This choice describes invasive lobular carcinoma.
Mucinous carcinoma has groups of tumor cells floating in extracellular mucin. The pink centers here are necrotic cores within expanded ducts. This choice describes mucinous carcinoma.
questions.explanation: The atypical cells rim expanded ducts with central necrosis, supporting comedo type ductal carcinoma in situ in this example. The companion mammogram illustrates why this pattern can be detected by branching microcalcifications.
visual_clues: Look for ducts rimmed by atypical cells around dense necrotic centers.

questions.condition_overview: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a malignant proliferation of ductal epithelial cells confined by the basement membrane. Patterns include comedo (high grade with central necrosis and calcifications), solid, cribriform, and papillary. It is usually detected as mammographic microcalcifications. Left untreated, a proportion progresses to invasive ductal carcinoma. Treatment is lumpectomy with radiation, or mastectomy, and endocrine therapy if ER positive.

questions.condition_overview: Invasive ductal carcinoma, no special type, is the most common breast cancer (about 75 percent). It presents as a hard, irregular, fixed mass with stellate borders that may cause skin dimpling or nipple retraction. Cords, nests, and glands of atypical cells infiltrate a desmoplastic stroma. It is graded by tubule formation, nuclear grade, and mitotic rate, and receptor status (ER, PR, HER2) guides therapy. It spreads to axillary nodes, bone, lung, liver, and brain.

questions.condition_overview: Serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC) is a noninvasive precursor lesion of high-grade serous carcinoma found in the fallopian tube, usually in the fimbria. Crowded, stratified secretory cells with enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei, loss of polarity, and mitoses replace the normal lining, with a strongly aberrant p53 pattern and high Ki-67. It is often found in women with BRCA mutations. This led to opportunistic salpingectomy as a risk-reducing strategy.

options: Both operations remove the tubes and ovaries.
Operation A removes potential tubal precursor tissue while preserving the ovaries.
Operation A removes the ovaries and leaves potential tubal precursor tissue in place.
Operation B leaves both fallopian tubes in place.

choice_rationales: Only the bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy in row B removes the ovaries. Opportunistic salpingectomy in row A removes potential tubal precursor tissue while preserving the ovaries. This choice describes a bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.

The table records that both tubes are removed in operation B. This choice describes an operation that leaves both tubes in place.

Both operations remove the fallopian tubes, including potential tubal precursor sites for high-grade serous carcinoma. Only operation B also removes the ovaries. This choice describes a procedure that removes no tubal tissue.
questions.explanation: The operation in row A removes both fallopian tubes and leaves the ovaries in place. The lecture connects this to the tubal origin of many high-grade serous cancers. questions.lead_in: The guide uses CDX2 to assess colorectal origin and calretinin to assess mesothelial origin. How do this patient’s results weigh those two alternatives?
questions.stem: The guide uses CDX2 to assess colorectal origin and calretinin to assess mesothelial origin. How do this patient’s results weigh those two alternatives?
options: The colorectal alternative is supported while the mesothelial alternative is less supported
The mesothelial alternative is supported while the colorectal alternative is less supported
Both alternatives are supported because both relevant stains are positive
Both alternatives are less supported because both relevant stains are negative
The colorectal alternative can be evaluated but the mesothelial marker was not measured
choice_rationales: CDX2 is negative, so the panel does not support a colorectal primary through that marker. Calretinin is also negative, weakening the mesothelial alternative. This choice describes a colorectal primary favored over a mesothelial one.

Calretinin is negative, weakening the mesothelial alternative. Negative CDX2 likewise supplies no support for a colorectal primary. This choice describes a mesothelial origin favored over a colorectal one.
CDX2 and calretinin are both negative in the effusion. These results weigh against colorectal and mesothelial origin, respectively. This choice describes support for both origins.

Negative CDX2 and calretinin weaken the colorectal and mesothelial alternatives, respectively. The combined positive pattern supports Müllerian origin in the case. This choice describes neither a colorectal nor a mesothelial origin (CDX2 and calretinin both negative), which is what the image shows.
The panel includes a measured negative calretinin result, which weakens the mesothelial alternative. CDX2 was also measured and is negative. This choice describes an unmeasured mesothelial marker.

Two smooth ovaries without visible surface lesions

questions.condition_overview: Epithelial ovarian cancer arises from the ovarian surface epithelium or fallopian tube and includes serous, endometrioid, clear cell, and mucinous types. It is often silent until advanced, with ascites and omental disease. Ultrasound shows complex solid and cystic masses with papillary projections, and CA-125 is often elevated. Staging is surgical, and treatment is cytoreductive surgery with platinum-based chemotherapy.
